story: Ziusudra was king of Shuruppak, having inherited rulership from his father Ubara-Tutu. Before this time, the first cities—Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larak, Sippar, and Shuruppak—had been founded. The gods decided to send a flood to destroy mankind, and the god Enki warned Ziusudra to build a large boat. A terrible storm raged for seven days, tossing the huge boat upon the great waters. Then the sun-god Utu appeared, and Ziusudra opened a window, prostrated himself, and sacrificed an ox and a sheep. After the flood subsided, Ziusudra prostrated himself before the sky god An and the god Enlil, who granted him eternal breath and took him to dwell in Dilmun, the place where the sun rises. Afterward, the flood swept over the land, and when it ended, kingship descended again from heaven and came to rest in the city of Kish. In another telling of this story, the hero was called Xisuthros, son of Ardates, said to have reigned for eighteen great cycles of years. In this version, the god Enki was identified with the god Cronus, father of Zeus, and the reed boat built by Xisuthros was said to have survived long afterward in the Corcyrean Mountains of Armenia.
blind: A ruler governed a city, having inherited rulership from his father, a former ruler. Before this time, the first cities had been founded. The divine beings decided to send a flood to destroy humankind, and a god of fresh waters warned the ruler to build a large boat. A terrible storm raged for seven days, tossing the huge boat upon the great waters. Then a sun deity appeared, and the ruler opened a window, prostrated himself, and sacrificed two kinds of livestock. After the flood subsided, the ruler prostrated himself before a sky god and another high god, who granted him eternal breath and took him to dwell in a distant paradise-land where the sun rises. Afterward, the flood swept over the land, and when it ended, kingship descended again from the heavens and came to rest in another city. In another telling of this story, the hero bore a different name, son of another figure, and was said to have reigned for eighteen great cycles of years. In this version, the god of fresh waters was identified with another deity, father of the chief sky god of a foreign pantheon, and the reed boat built by the hero was said to have survived long afterward in a distant mountain range.
title: Ziusudra
